description: MVM - a few engineers who thought a space hackathon sounded fun. Now we’ve got a weekend to make something work.
summary:
Working with SAR data comes with two practical challenges: accessing it and understanding what it tells us. For this challenge, we set out to build a tool that helps people without a technical background explore and interpret data from the NISAR mission.
Our website, sar.packetlab.pl, lets users select an area of interest, view the available radar observations, and compare them over a chosen time period. This makes it easier to see where and when the measurements have changed.
details:
SAR Change Explorer is an interactive web application that helps people explore how Earth’s surface changes over time using NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations. It turns complex satellite files into an accessible globe with a timeline, original radar imagery, and clear change overlays.

Users can explore the prepared Poznań study area or draw a rectangle anywhere on the map and request available observations for a chosen date range. The server searches NASA’s catalogue, checks for compatible acquisitions covering the selected area, and downloads the required portions of the source files. It processes valid radar measurements onto a common analysis grid and compares each observation with the first acquisition in the selected series.

The map highlights backscatter decreases in blue and increases in orange, using a 3 dB threshold. Users can place the original grayscale radar image beneath these highlights to inspect their context. A compact timeline shows actual acquisition dates, while country borders, cities, roads, and rivers help users locate areas of interest. Up to five successfully processed regions remain available during the browser session. An optional NASA POWER panel adds temperature and precipitation context near the selected region.

The project’s intended impact is to make radar data easier to explore for students, educators, researchers, and curious members of the public. It can help users identify patterns worth investigating, such as changes around agricultural land, waterways, or urban areas. These highlights are starting points for investigation: a radar change alone does not establish flooding, damage, or its cause.

Our creative approach combines scientific traceability with familiar map interactions. Users can move between dates and regions, inspect the underlying radar image, and view source identifiers and processing limitations without handling large scientific files themselves. Imagery and date labels update together, preventing an observation from appearing under the wrong date.

The application uses JavaScript, HTML, and CSS with CesiumJS and Vite. Python processing uses NumPy, GDAL, h5py, and Pillow. OpenStreetMap-derived road data and Natural Earth geography provide map context. Caddy serves the application, and automated Python and Playwright tests check processing, request handling, and browser behaviour. Development and testing used a conventional desktop computer, without dedicated GPU computing. OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assisted with design, debugging, testing, documentation, and interface project.

We considered scientific comparability, missing data, provisional product limitations, processing time, memory use, and clear communication of uncertainty. Requested NASA data and generated results are held in temporary server workspaces and deleted after delivery, cancellation, or failure. Successfully loaded regions remain in browser memory for the open session, avoiding a persistent server-side results cache.
